High Point enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 30-4 overall and 15-1 in Big South play after winning the Big South tournament title over Winthrop, 91-76, on March 8, 2026. The Panthers finished the regular season 27-4 and 15-1 in league play, then added conference-tournament wins over Gardner-Webb (81-59 on March 6), UNC Asheville (75-71 on March 7), and Winthrop (91-76 on March 8). Their statistical profile is loud and specific: 91.8 points per game, 50.1% from the field, 36.0% from three, and regular-season national top-25 marks in steals per game (11.1), turnover margin (+7.5), fastbreak points (19.16), scoring offense (90.7), assist/turnover ratio (1.78), and effective field-goal percentage (57.1). ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2026/3/5/mens-basketball-clayman-named-2025-26-joe-b-hall-finalist.aspx))

Offensively, High Point plays fast, but not recklessly. The scheme is built around guard Rob Martin initiating, wings running lanes, and frontcourt players who can both finish and pass. The numbers prove the ball movement is real: High Point has 512 assists on 871 made field goals, Martin leads the team with 121 assists (3.7 per game), Conrad Martinez has 116 (3.4), and center/forward Owen Aquino has 82 (2.4). That tells you this is not a one-guard pound-the-air-out system; they run through multiple decision-makers. Specific actions show up repeatedly in game recaps: against Furman on November 3, Martinez scored on a floater and then a transition three created by Cam'Ron Fletcher’s push-ahead pass, while Martin later found Aquino for a dunk; against Winthrop on February 21, Vincent Brady II and Fletcher connected on alley-oop actions and Aquino spaced to hit an early wing three; against UNC Asheville on March 7, Martin collapsed two defenders and kicked to Chase Johnston for a right-wing dagger three with 1:07 left. Those are named examples of their actual play diet: drag-screen transition creation, drive-and-kick spacing, lob actions, and inside-out reads through Aquino and Anderson. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2025/11/4/mens-basketball-panthers-victorious-in-field-of-68-opening-day-marathon.aspx))

Their scoring balance is the engine. Terry Anderson leads the team at 16.0 points per game on 56.4% shooting, Martin adds 15.3, Fletcher 12.7, Aquino 9.4, Martinez 9.3, and Scotty Washington 8.7. Johnston is the elite spacer at 48.5% from three on 64 makes, while Braden Hausen has hit 54 threes. The result is a roster that can score in layers: post seals and rim attacks from Anderson, advantage creation from Martin, second-side shooting from Johnston and Hausen, and vertical athleticism from Fletcher and Caden Miller. The Radford game on January 23 is the best single-game example of the offense when it is humming: Anderson went for a career-high 31 points and 12 rebounds, earned 14 free-throw attempts, and carried them through a 10-point second-half comeback in a 93-83 road win. The February 21 Winthrop win shows the spacing version of the same offense: with the game tied 73-73, Fletcher hit back-to-back threes, then Hausen hit a corner three off a Martin pass to put High Point in control. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Defensively, High Point is a pressure program. Flynn Clayman said after the season-opening 97-71 win over Furman that the Panthers had 50 deflections, and the season data supports that emphasis: 323 steals as a team, Martin at 1.6 steals per game, Martinez 1.5, Anderson 1.4, Aquino 1.2, Fletcher 1.2, and the regular-season note that High Point ranked first nationally in steals per game and turnover margin while third in turnovers forced. This is not passive positional defense. They jump passing lanes, dig at drives, and try to turn live-ball takeaways into transition points. Furman committed 22 turnovers in the opener, and High Point converted those into a 13-1 first-half edge in points off turnovers. UIC committed 18 turnovers on November 20, while High Point held UIC to 21.7% from three. The strongest proof that they can also defend in the half court came February 19 against UNC Asheville: High Point won 74-48, and Clayman called it “about as good of a defensive performance as I’ve ever coached,” with Asheville held to its fewest points against HPU since 2011. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2025/11/4/mens-basketball-panthers-victorious-in-field-of-68-opening-day-marathon.aspx))

Clayman’s coaching philosophy is continuity plus sharper defensive accountability. He took over for Alan Huss for the 2025-26 season and immediately preserved the aggressive, high-possession style while leaning even harder into pressure, deflections, and transition offense. His Furman quote emphasized offseason shot-tracker work and defensive effort, which fits the statistical profile. More important, there is documented evidence of in-game adjustment. At Radford on January 23, Clayman said High Point was “sloppy” in its game-plan execution early, but the Panthers adjusted, cleaned up the attack, and reversed a 10-point second-half deficit behind Anderson’s interior dominance and better decision-making. After the February 21 win over Winthrop, Clayman said, “Early in the year we would’ve lost that game 100%,” which is a direct statement that the team’s late-game poise improved during the season. Another strong adjustment example came January 10 at Charleston Southern: after a tying jumper with 2.3 seconds left in regulation forced overtime, High Point steadied itself, got a go-ahead Martinez three in OT, then closed with an Anderson layup and Aquino free throws to win 84-82. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2025/11/4/mens-basketball-panthers-victorious-in-field-of-68-opening-day-marathon.aspx))

Clutch execution is mostly a strength, and the exact games matter. In the Big South semifinal against UNC Asheville on March 7, Johnston hit the biggest shot of the game, a right-wing three with 1:07 left for a 71-62 lead, and the Panthers then made four free throws in the final 44 seconds to close a 75-71 win. In the regular-season clincher against Winthrop on February 21, the Panthers were tied 73-73 with 4:30 left; Fletcher hit back-to-back threes, Hausen made a clutch corner three with 1:30 left, and High Point survived 89-87. At Charleston Southern on January 10, Martin scored 20, Martinez hit the key overtime three, and Aquino’s two free throws stretched the lead to 84-79 with 1:33 left before High Point won 84-82. There is one important warning sign: on December 14 against App State, High Point led 70-64 with 1:13 left in regulation and still lost 86-78 in overtime after allowing a tying layup with one second left. That game exposed that late-clock containment can crack if the initial pressure does not end the possession. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-hpu-advances-to-big-south-championship-game-for-second-straight-year.aspx))

The key players each have a defined scouting role. Anderson is the primary scorer and most reliable matchup problem: 16.0 points, 56.4% shooting, career-high 31 points and 12 rebounds at Radford on January 23, then 25 points and 12 rebounds in the March 7 semifinal and 18 points in the March 8 title game. Martin is the lead guard and tempo-setter: 15.3 points, 3.7 assists, 1.6 steals, 24 points and seven assists in the Big South title game, 20 points at Charleston Southern, and a season-high 27 at USC Upstate on February 12. Aquino is the defensive anchor and connective big: 9.4 points, 6.0 rebounds, 2.4 assists, 1.7 blocks, 58 total blocks, and 45.5% from three on 15 makes. Martinez is the bench creator: 9.3 points and 3.4 assists, with a career-high 26 points versus La Salle on December 19 and 11 assists against App State on December 14. Fletcher is the swing athlete: 12.7 points on 54.8% shooting, plus a massive 17-point, 19-rebound game in the conference championship. Johnston is the shooting specialist defenses cannot help off, with 64 made threes at 48.5% and the semifinal dagger versus Asheville. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The notable wins and losses reveal the ceiling and the vulnerability. Best wins: Furman 97-71 on November 3 showed the offense was already organized in Clayman’s first game; Gardner-Webb 104-49 on January 7 was the largest margin over a Division I and conference opponent in Big South history; Radford 93-83 on January 23 showed comeback toughness; Winthrop 89-87 on February 21 showed clutch shot-making under pressure; and Winthrop 91-76 on March 8 showed they could dominate the league’s best challenger on a title stage. The losses are instructive too. UAB beat High Point 91-74 on November 14, exposing defensive slippage against stronger athletes. Southern Illinois beat them 86-84 on December 3, showing they can be dragged into a close-possession game. App State beat them 86-78 in overtime on December 14 after High Point led by six in the final 73 seconds. Winthrop beat them 92-75 on January 14, proving that if an opponent handles the pressure and wins the physical exchanges, High Point can look ordinary; the Panthers’ answer was to beat Winthrop twice afterward, which is one of their best adjustment markers. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/news/2025/11/4/mens-basketball-panthers-victorious-in-field-of-68-opening-day-marathon.aspx))

On head-coach NCAA tournament history: Flynn Clayman is making his first NCAA tournament appearance as a head coach in 2026. The previous High Point head coach, Alan Huss, led the Panthers to the 2025 NCAA Tournament, the first Division I NCAA berth in program history. Huss’s official High Point bio documents a 2023-24 season ending in the Big South semifinals and a run to the 2024 CBI championship game, then the 2025 NCAA berth before he departed. Huss had no prior NCAA tournament history as a head coach before High Point; his NCAA tournament history before that was as a Creighton player on teams that reached the field in 1999, 2000, and 2001. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/alan-huss/1670))

High Point enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile as a classic mid-major tension case: the raw team performance is excellent, the predictive rankings are mixed-to-solid, and the résumé metrics are held down hard by one of the weakest schedules in the country. As of games through March 15, High Point is 27-4 in Division I games, 15-1 in the Big South, with a NET rank of 75. WarrenNolan’s comparison page lists the Panthers at BPI No. 63, KenPom/POM No. 92, and Bart Torvik T-Rank No. 93, while their result-based metrics sit at KPI No. 96, SOR No. 66, and WAB No. 69. In other words, résumé says “good mid-major,” BPI says “dangerous enough,” and possession-based systems are more skeptical than the win-loss record alone would suggest. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=High-Point))

The first thing that jumps out is just how weak the schedule has been. High Point’s NET strength of schedule is 363 nationally, and its non-conference NET SOS is 361. WarrenNolan’s team sheet also gives them an RPI SOS of 331 and non-conference RPI SOS of 311. That is a massive anchor on every résumé discussion. The quadrant distribution tells the story cleanly: 0-0 in Q1, 0-2 in Q2, 5-2 in Q3, and 22-0 in Q4. So this is not a team that built its profile on high-end wins; it is a team that relentlessly beat the teams it was supposed to beat, almost never slipped against the bottom of the schedule, and dominated a low-leverage path. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=High-Point))

From a statistical-performance standpoint, though, High Point is legitimately potent. TeamRankings has the Panthers at 86.5 points per game, No. 10 nationally, with a +14.6 scoring margin, No. 8 nationally. The school’s official cumulative stats are even gaudier on a full-games basis: 90.0 points per game, 70.3 allowed, and a +19.7 margin over 34 games. TeamRankings shows an offensive effective field goal rate of 54.7 percent, which ranks No. 48 nationally, while High Point’s official season totals imply an eFG% of 56.6 percent from 1,034 field goals and 314 threes on 2,104 attempts. That gap is likely a timing/sample difference between data providers, but both sources agree on the broad point: this is a highly efficient shooting offense, especially inside the arc. TeamRankings has High Point at 57.1 percent on twos, No. 33 nationally, versus 34.4 percent from three, only No. 156. That is important analytically: the Panthers are not an elite bombing team so much as a team that scores efficiently because it converts twos, gets to the line, and avoids empty possessions. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/team/high-point-panthers/stats))

The Four Factors profile reinforces that interpretation. High Point’s offense posts a 54.7 percent eFG, a 11.2 percent turnover rate, and a 30.7 percent offensive rebound rate according to TeamRankings. Its free-throw rate is excellent: TeamRankings lists FTA/FGA at 0.429, No. 22 nationally, and the official team stats yield a nearly identical 0.433 from 911 free-throw attempts against 2,104 field-goal attempts. Their 3-point attempt rate is moderate-high rather than extreme: TeamRankings gives 26.3 threes attempted per 61.2 field-goal attempts, about 0.430, while the official stat line is 883 threes on 2,104 shots, about 0.420. So High Point does take a healthy number of threes, but the identity is more balanced than a pure spread-and-bomb offense. The true efficiency drivers are foul pressure, ball security, and two-point finishing. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/team/high-point-panthers/stats))

Defensively, the profile is less overwhelming than the record suggests, which helps explain why KenPom and Torvik are more conservative than BPI. TeamRankings gives High Point an opponent eFG% of 50.1 percent, No. 105 nationally, and opponent two-point percentage of 51.6 percent, No. 176. Opponents also rebound 30.0 percent of their misses, while High Point’s defensive rebounding rate is only 70.0 percent, No. 256. Those are not dominant half-court defense numbers. What rescues the defense is turnover creation: opponents turn it over on 19.0 percent of plays, No. 5 nationally, and High Point averages 10.4 steals per game, No. 1 nationally. That creates a feast-or-famine look. The Panthers can blow teams open with live-ball takeaways and transition scoring, but the underlying shot-defense and glass-control indicators are more ordinary. That is precisely the kind of statistical split that can diverge from the eye test: if you watch High Point overwhelm Big South opponents, it can look like a suffocating defense; the possession data says it is more a turnover-pressure defense than a shot-suppression defense. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/team/high-point-panthers/stats))

Possession pace is harder to pin down exactly from broadly accessible public sources in this search set, and an exact possessions-per-40 figure was not exposed cleanly. But the available evidence points to a fast, offense-forward team. High Point scores at a top-10 national per-game level, attempts 61.2 field goals and 26.3 threes per game, forces turnovers at an elite rate, and produces a large scoring margin. That combination strongly suggests an above-average pace with an emphasis on early offense and transition opportunities created by steals, even if a precise possessions-per-40 number was not directly available from the sources surfaced here. ([teamrankings.com](https://www.teamrankings.com/ncaa-basketball/team/high-point-panthers/stats))

Recent-form and trend data are also imperfectly accessible in exact top-line efficiency form, but the record context is strong. High Point is 30-4 overall on its official page and 27-4 in Division I games on WarrenNolan, with a 22-0 Q4 record and only four total Division I losses. The shape of the season implies a stable high floor against weaker competition rather than a volatile boom-bust profile. What we can say confidently is that there is no evidence in the available data of a late collapse; instead, the Panthers carried an elite win rate into March while continuing to post strong scoring margins. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

So the analytical bottom line is this: High Point is better than the dismissive “just a small-conference team with a padded record” take, but also less battle-tested than the gaudy record and point differential imply. The offense is real: strong eFG, elite foul drawing, excellent turnover avoidance, and top-tier scoring volume. The defense is more conditional: elite at forcing mistakes, much less dominant at controlling shot quality and the defensive glass. The biggest divergence from conventional wisdom is that High Point does not project like a pure Cinderella shot-making heater. It projects more like a structurally sound, pressure-heavy, downhill offense that can absolutely stress a favorite if the game tilts into turnover chaos and free-throw volume. The biggest caution is equally clear: because the schedule has been so soft, every metric built on opponent adjustment is asking whether those advantages will hold once the Panthers face high-major size, athleticism, and half-court execution. The answer from the numbers is not “no” — but it is definitely “prove it on a bigger stage.” ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=High-Point))
matchup-analyst:
High Point enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as an offense-first team that plays fast, spreads the floor with multiple interchangeable 6-6 to 6-8 forwards, and punishes mistakes with steals and immediate conversion. The raw profile is elite for a mid-major: 90.0 points per game, .491 team field-goal percentage, 16.3 assists per game, only 9.4 turnovers per game, and 21.2 points off turnovers forced. Defensively, they generate 10.9 steals per game while forcing 16.4 opponent turnovers. That statistical combination tells you exactly what they want: pace, live-ball chaos, and efficient finishing once they get an advantage. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Their core style is built around balanced scoring rather than one heliocentric creator. Rob Martin leads the backcourt creation with 121 assists in 33 games, or 3.7 per game, while Conrad Martinez adds 116 assists in 34 games, or 3.4 per game. In the frontcourt, Terry Anderson is the primary pressure point scorer at 181 made field goals, 165 made free throws, 14.5 points per game, and 6.0 rebounds per game; Owen Aquino adds interior finishing and rim protection with 116 made field goals, 199 rebounds, and 58 blocks; Cam’Ron Fletcher gives them another slashing, rebounding forward at 6-7 with 6.9 rebounds per game. Their roster is specifically built to play big on the wing: Martin is 5-10, Martinez 6-0, but then Anderson is 6-6, Aquino 6-8, Fletcher 6-7, Hausen 6-7, and Johnston is a 6-3 spacer. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

If you are asking what disrupts High Point’s offense, the clearest answer is this: take away clean early offense, keep them out of the paint-to-kick game, and make their half-court guards score over size without transition help. In the 86-84 loss to Southern Illinois on December 3, 2025, High Point still scored 84, but SIU won by posting 24 fast-break points, 40 paint points, and 42 rebounds while forcing High Point’s guards into a more fragmented scoring game. Martin scored 20, Anderson 21, but High Point only had 12 fast-break points and Martinez went 2-for-8 with three turnovers. That is the template: physicality at the point of attack and no easy run-outs. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/southern-illinois/boxscore/15956))

Appalachian State provided another usable anti-High Point blueprint in the 86-78 win over the Panthers on December 14, 2025. High Point launched 44 threes, their season high in a game, and shot just 8-for-30 from deep overall in the box score section for key rotation players shown in the starter-heavy lines: Martin was 1-for-4 from three, Fletcher 0-for-6, Johnston 1-for-4, Martinez 1-for-7, and Anderson 3-for-7. Even though High Point still generated 30 paint points and 13 fast-break points, App State kept them from turning that into overall efficiency by holding them to 78 points, winning the possession game late, and forcing their half-court execution to become jumper-heavy. When High Point is baited into volume threes without rhythm, their offense is materially less dangerous. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/appalachian-state/boxscore/15958))

On press vulnerability specifically, the available season data points more to High Point being strong against pressure than weak against it. Their season turnover average is only 9.4 per game, and they finished with a 1.7 assist-to-turnover ratio. Martin posted a 2.37 assist/turnover ratio, Martinez 2.90, Hausen 2.80, and Vincent Brady II 2.67. That means a full-court press that is merely disruptive, not turnover-producing, is actually dangerous against them because it can feed their preferred transition game. The better tactic is not gambling press but selective containment pressure: make Martin and Martinez bring it up versus length, then flatten into a packed shell in the half court. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Zone vulnerability is more real than press vulnerability, especially if the zone is long and closes driving gaps without overhelping on the first kick-out. The App State loss is the best evidence because High Point was pushed toward perimeter volume, attempting 44 threes, the team’s high against a Division I opponent listed on its cumulative stats page. Southern Illinois also succeeded by allowing only 84 despite High Point’s normal offensive baseline of 90.0 per game, again suggesting that opponents who wall off the lane and force secondary shooters into contested jumpers can drag them below their norm. That said, you cannot play a soft zone: High Point has real shooting on the floor with Chase Johnston at .485 from three, Scotty Washington at .382, Braden Hausen at .358, Conrad Martinez at .339, and Martin capable of volume even at a lower percentage. The right zone is an active matchup zone with long closeouts, not a passive 2-3. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Preferred pace: High Point clearly wants games in the 80s and 90s. They scored 91 against Winthrop in the Big South final, 89 against Winthrop on February 21, 93 at Radford, and 87 at UNC Asheville in the league opener. In those games, they repeatedly won by converting transition or semi-transition chances: 24 fast-break points against Winthrop on February 21, 13 in the title game against Winthrop, and 6 in a more controlled game at UNC Asheville, where their scoring leaned more into paint offense. To force the opposite, you must cut off live-ball turnovers first and offensive rebounds second. High Point averages 21.2 points off turnovers; if you reduce those free points, you make them play longer half-court possessions against a set defense. ([dxbhsrqyrr690.cloudfront.net](https://dxbhsrqyrr690.cloudfront.net/sidearm.nextgen.sites/highpointpanthers.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/20260221054711-2713372.pdf))

Position-by-position mismatch notes matter. At point guard, Martin is only 5-10, 170; bigger guards can shoot over him and switch him into post entries or force him to finish over length. Martinez at 6-0, 175 has similar size concerns. On the wing, High Point flips the script: Terry Anderson is a 6-6 forward with guard-like usage and drew 218 free throws this season, while Fletcher is 6-7, 220 and can overwhelm smaller 3s and 4s on the glass. Aquino at 6-8, 230 is the one true interior anchor, but if your 5 can drag him into space, you can attack his mobility while also putting foul pressure on him; he committed 89 fouls, most on the team. The flip side is that High Point can become vulnerable against real high-major frontcourt size because their main rebound-and-rim group is Aquino/Fletcher/Anderson rather than a true two-big lineup. Winthrop’s Logan Duncomb got 23 points and 14 rebounds against them on February 21, and Winthrop had 46 paint points that day even in a loss. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/2025-26))

Isolation versus team offense: this is more team offense than isolation. High Point logged 554 assists on 1,034 made field goals, meaning about 53.6% of their makes were assisted. They also averaged 16.3 assists per game with two primary table-setters in Martin and Martinez, plus a facilitating big in Aquino with 82 assists. That said, late-clock or momentum-possession offense often shifts to Anderson, whose free-throw volume and paint scoring make him their best bailout option. His 31-point game at Radford is the cleanest example: over a 3:09 stretch in the second half, he outscored Radford 8-5 by himself, then added another 8 of High Point’s next 11 points to close separation. So the macro tendency is team offense, but the micro late-game tendency is Anderson isolation or power drives. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Transition offense and defense frequency are reflected indirectly but convincingly in the game and season data. High Point scores 21.2 points off turnovers and creates 10.9 steals per game, which is a major transition profile. In specific games they produced 24 fast-break points versus Winthrop on February 21, 13 in the conference title game, 13 against Appalachian State even in a loss, and 6 at UNC Asheville in a more controlled conference opener. On the other side, when opponents run successfully, High Point can be hit: Southern Illinois posted 24 fast-break points in its win, and Winthrop scored 13 fast-break points in the February 21 near-upset while also getting 46 paint points. That says High Point is dangerous in transition but not invulnerable defending it, especially if opponents get through the first layer of ball pressure. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))

Coaching adaptability: there is evidence the staff can adjust within games, though the user asked about “mid-series,” which does not really apply in college basketball single-elimination settings. A better proxy is repeat-opponent adjustment. Against Winthrop on February 21, High Point won 89-87 while allowing 46 paint points and 22 second-chance points; in the March 8 title game rematch, High Point held Winthrop to 35.7% shooting, 24.2% from three, and only 34 paint points while winning 91-76. That is a concrete improvement against the same opponent in less than three weeks. The staff also showed tactical flexibility in lineup usage: in the title game, Fletcher came off the bench and delivered 17 points and 19 rebounds in 29 minutes, while Johnston provided 11 points on 3-for-3 from three in 22 minutes. That looks like a staff willing to alter minute distribution and role emphasis based on matchup and game flow. ([dxbhsrqyrr690.cloudfront.net](https://dxbhsrqyrr690.cloudfront.net/sidearm.nextgen.sites/highpointpanthers.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/20260221054711-2713372.pdf))

Concrete game plan: To beat this team you must do four things. First, do not feed their transition game: target 12 or fewer turnovers because High Point averages 21.2 points off turnovers and 10.9 steals per game. Second, force them into jump-shot volume without catch-and-shoot rhythm by shrinking gaps on Anderson and Fletcher drives, then rotating hard to Johnston and Hausen; App State’s win after High Point’s 44 three-point attempts is the clearest model. Third, attack their small guards and their foul-prone frontcourt physically: Martin is 5-10, Martinez is 6-0, and Aquino leads the team with 89 fouls. Fourth, finish possessions with defensive rebounds, because if High Point gets extra possessions and live-ball steals, the game drifts immediately into the 80s and 90s where they are most comfortable. If you can hold them to a half-court, 68-to-72 possession feel, keep Anderson off the foul line, and make Martin/Martinez score over length instead of creating paint collapse, you give yourself the best chance to knock them out. ([highpointpanthers.com](https://highpointpanthers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats))
